title: Dreaming Versus Expecting
text:
Popular advice often says that picturing success will help you achieve it. The psychologist Gabriele Oettingen, working in Germany, had doubts. In a 2002 paper with Doris Mayer, she separated two ways of thinking about the future: expectations, judgments of how likely success is based on past experience, and fantasies, pleasant images of the desired future that come to mind.

In one study, university graduates about to look for a job reported how likely they thought they were to find one, and also described the thoughts and images that came to them when they imagined their job search. Two years later the researchers followed up. Graduates with high expectations had done well. But those whose fantasies were the most positive, who pictured themselves sailing smoothly into an ideal job, had sent out fewer applications, received fewer offers and were earning less than those with more mixed or sober images.

Similar patterns appeared in other studies in the paper: among students hoping to start a relationship with someone they had a crush on, among students hoping to do well on an exam, and among patients recovering from hip replacement surgery. Positive expectations predicted more effort and better outcomes. Positive fantasies predicted less.

Oettingen argued that pleasant fantasies let the mind enjoy the goal in advance, which drains the energy needed to pursue it. She later developed a method called mental contrasting, which pairs the imagined goal with the obstacles in the way.
lesson: Enjoy imagining the goal, but do not stop there. Picture the main obstacle that stands in your way and plan how you will deal with it; that is what turns a dream into effort.
source: Oettingen, G., and Mayer, D. (2002). The motivating function of thinking about the future: Expectations versus fantasies. Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, 83(5), 1198-1212.
